questions.stem: You are the architect on an insurance claims assistant. Discovery has produced three statements: 'we want to reduce claim handling time by 30%', 'the adjusters want fewer summaries', and 'compliance needs an audit trail for every recommendation'. Which discovery activity would most improve the quality of the resulting specification?

options.text: Push on what the 30% figure is measured against today - current handling time, current summaries produced, current recommendation logging - because a target that cannot be compared to a measured baseline is not a requirement, and each stakeholder group is describing a different slice of the same process.
Ask each stakeholder group to rank the three statements by business value, so the specification reflects the most important requirement.
Ask each group to estimate the effort they expect to save, and treat the group with the largest estimate as the primary beneficiary.
Draft the specification now and circulate it for comment, since a concrete artefact gets more useful feedback than open questions.

questions.explanation:
The three statements are not three requirements - they are three **partial views** of one process, and the specification is what makes them into a coherent one. The highest-value discovery move is establishing the baseline, because it converts an aspiration into something testable.

'Reduce handling time by 30%' is unusable until you know current handling time and what is counted. 'Fewer summaries' is unusable until you know how many are produced and what an adjuster does with them today. 'An audit trail for every recommendation' is the most concrete of the three, and it may conflict with the other two - an audit trail that logs the evidence considered for each recommendation costs work, and if it is not specified carefully it will either be useless or prohibitively slow.

That last point is why baselines matter architecturally and not just for reporting: once each statement has a number attached, the conflicts become visible and arguable. Right now the fastest way to specification is to make the claims measurable.

The rejected options each substitute a mechanism for a specification. Ranking and effort estimates tell you who feels strongly, not what to build, and a draft spec circulated before baselines exist just relocates the vagueness into a document people now feel obliged to review.

whyWrong.B: Ranking produces a priority order, not a specification. 'Fewer summaries' outranking 'audit trail' does not tell you whether 30% is measured end to end or per claim, and the highest-ranked statement can still be unusable as written.
whyWrong.C: Effort estimates measure enthusiasm, not value, and they systematically favour whoever has the loudest pain. Nothing in the method connects an estimate to the 30% target or to what the system must do.
whyWrong.D: A concrete artefact does get better feedback than open questions - but only once its content is decidable. Circulating a spec built on unmeasured claims collects opinions about ambiguity rather than resolving it.

questions.mindset: Before specifying, make each claim measurable - a target you cannot compare to a baseline is not a requirement.

questions.stem: A retailer's VP of Operations says: 'just use the best Claude model, we don't want to think about tiers.' The CFO says: 'our margin on returns processing is thin.' A security architect warns that a tier upgrade changes latency and cost per call. Which response best advances discovery?

options.text: Surface the disagreement as what it is - an unpriced quality decision - and ask each of them to name the number that would change their position: which accuracy shortfall at the cheaper tier would be unacceptable, and what cost per return processing would justify it. Discovery here is eliciting the trade-off, not resolving it by fiat.
Take the VP's instruction literally and specify the most capable tier. The executive sponsor's stated preference settles the question, and the CFO's concern is a finance matter for later.
Split the difference by specifying a mid-tier model, which satisfies both stakeholders partially and avoids an escalation.
Run a two-week bake-off across tiers on real returns data and present the results, letting the numbers settle the question without further discussion.

questions.explanation:
Three stakeholders, three legitimate priorities, and no shared basis for choosing. That is a **discovery** situation, not an escalation or a benchmarking situation.

The useful move is to make the trade-off explicit and priced. Ask the VP what accuracy shortfall at a cheaper tier would be unacceptable - that converts 'best model' into a quality bar. Ask the CFO what cost per return processing the business case tolerates - that converts 'margin is thin' into a number. Now there is a decision to make with two named thresholds, and the security architect's latency concern fits as a third constraint rather than an interruption.

Option D is tempting and wrong for a specific reason: a bake-off before anyone has said what they are optimising for produces three more numbers nobody can interpret. Which metric wins? The bake-off becomes its own stakeholder conflict, two weeks later.

Worth noting what C actually does - it picks a compromise nobody argued for, on the theory that splitting the difference avoids conflict. It usually relocates the conflict rather than settling it, and it leaves nobody able to say why the tier was chosen.

whyWrong.B: Executive preference does not settle a question that has a cost and quality dimension attached. The CFO's constraint is not a later finance matter; it is one of the inputs that determines whether this project is viable at all.
whyWrong.C: A compromise nobody argued for is not consensus. It avoids the conversation now by removing the basis for a decision, and it produces a tier nobody can justify when the results come in.
whyWrong.D: Useful as a later step, wrong as a first one. Without knowing what each stakeholder is optimising for, the bake-off produces competing numbers rather than an answer - and two weeks is a long time to be the mechanism for a conversation that takes one.

questions.mindset: When stakeholders disagree on priorities, elicit their thresholds - that turns a preference war into a decision with numbers.

questions.stem: You have recommended a retrieval-based design over sending full documents to a large-context model. An executive asks why the apparently simpler option - one model, one prompt, whole document - was rejected. Which framing is most likely to hold up?

options.text: Give the quality and cost evidence on this firm's own documents - measured accuracy with and without retrieval, cost per document, and what happens to both as the corpus grows - and state what would change your recommendation, such as a specific accuracy gain that would justify the simpler design.

Explain that retrieval is the industry-standard architecture for this problem class, that large-context prompting is considered a fallback, and that the firm should follow established practice to reduce risk.
Explain that sending full documents consumes far more tokens and is therefore more expensive, without going into quality, since cost is the only factor the executive needs.
Offer to build the simple version first and revisit retrieval if accuracy disappoints, since starting simple is the safest way to keep the schedule.

questions.explanation:
An executive is deciding whether to trust a recommendation, and what builds that trust is **evidence from their situation plus an explicit reversal condition**.

Evidence from their own documents is what makes the argument theirs rather than a general principle. Quality is genuinely uncertain here and should be presented as measured on their data, not asserted - retrieval typically helps on large or noisy corpora, but that is an empirical claim, and the strongest version of your argument is your own measurement of it. Cost per document is the part that generalises cleanly, because it grows with corpus size in one design and not the other.

The reversal condition is what separates a recommendation from advocacy. Naming the specific accuracy gain that would justify the simple design tells the executive you have thought about what would change the answer - and it converts the conversation from 'do you trust me' into 'here is the decision and its trigger'.

The rejected options each fail a different test. B appeals to convention rather than evidence, which is weak with a technical executive and wrong as a matter of practice. C reduces a quality argument to cost. D offers to pre-commit to being wrong, framed as prudence.

whyWrong.B: Convention is not evidence, and 'industry standard' is contestable in exactly the area under discussion. An executive weighing a real cost against an uncertain quality claim should be given measurements, not consensus appeal.
whyWrong.C: Cost is real but partial, and presenting only cost invites the obvious objection. If cost were the whole story the simple design would often win - the argument only holds when quality evidence points the other way, so quality evidence belongs in it.
whyWrong.D: This commits to a design you have already argued against, and calls it prudence. If the measurement you expect has not been done, the risk is that 'accuracy disappoints' is discovered in production by the business.

questions.mindset: Recommend with your measurements and name the condition that would reverse it - that is trust, not advocacy.

questions.stem: A steering committee must choose between a fixed prompt chain that processes documents predictably at lower cost, and an agentic design that handles unexpected cases better at roughly double the cost. Which presentation is most likely to reach a decision?

options.text: Frame both on the criteria the committee set - cost per document, error cost by type, and time to implement - with your recommendation stated plainly alongside what the recommended option gives up and which measured result would change the decision.
Present the agentic design in depth and note the fixed chain as the fallback if budget becomes a problem, so the committee has one clear option to approve.
Present the cost comparison only, since cost is the criterion the finance representative attends to and the cheapest option wins a budget conversation.
Send the full technical comparison - prompt designs, tool schemas, orchestration diagrams - and let the committee identify the trade-off themselves.

questions.explanation:
A steering committee is not evaluating designs; it is **deciding against criteria it already owns**. The architect's job is to populate the criteria the committee set, not to introduce new ones. Cost per document, error cost by type, and time to implement are the terms the business is already using.

Two components of the recommended option are doing specific work. **What it gives up** protects against the failure mode where a recommendation is treated as a claim of universal superiority - naming the cost and the cases it handles worse makes it credible rather than promotional. **Which measured result would change the decision** gives the committee a trigger for revisiting, which is what converts a one-off approval into an ongoing arrangement.

The rejected options each remove the committee's ability to decide. B offers one option, so the meeting becomes ratification. C reduces a multi-criteria decision to the criterion with the loudest advocate - and error cost can plausibly exceed the cost difference on a small fraction of documents. D inverts the responsibility: the committee is being asked to do the analysis that justified hiring you.

whyWrong.B: Presenting one option in depth makes the meeting an approval ritual rather than a decision, and it removes the committee's ability to exercise judgement on a trade-off it owns.
whyWrong.C: The committee set multiple criteria and cost is not obviously decisive. On a small fraction of documents the error cost of the cheaper design can exceed the entire saving - that is precisely the calculation that needs to happen.
whyWrong.D: The committee lacks the context to evaluate tool schemas and orchestration diagrams, and is not in a position to derive the trade-off you were engaged to analyse. Shifting the analysis back is a way of avoiding the recommendation.

questions.mindset: Populate the criteria the committee owns, state what your recommendation gives up, and name the result that would change it.

questions.stem: A bank's operations manager ran the same loan-summary request twice and got differently worded summaries. She asks for a guarantee that 'identical inputs always give identical outputs'. Which response is most defensible?

options.text: Agree on what must be stable rather than that everything must be. The five extracted fields, the schema and the decision can be made consistent - with structured output and validation for the fields, and a documented tolerance for wording - while prose phrasing is non-deterministic by design and is not a guarantee you can give.
Promise byte-identical output by setting temperature to zero on every summarization request, since sampling is the only source of variation.
Agree to the guarantee and implement response caching, so the first answer for a given input is returned for every repeat request.
Decline any consistency commitment, since generative outputs are inherently non-deterministic and no SLA on output stability is technically possible.

questions.explanation:
The stakeholder has identified a real need - she cannot tell whether two runs of the same request are equally valid - but has expressed it as a guarantee that cannot be given. The architect's job is to **separate the part that matters from the part that is noise**, and then commit to the first.

In a loan summary, what a downstream process or a reviewer consumes is the extracted fields and the decision. Those *can* be made consistent: structured output constrains the shape, code-side validation enforces the fields, and business rules can require that a decision never flip without a stated reason. Phrasing is different - the model produces fluent text and will word it differently across runs, and that variation carries no information. So the right answer to the operations manager is a **defined consistency contract**: these five fields and this decision are consistent and validated; wording varies within a documented tolerance, and here is the tolerance.

B is the most common wrong answer and worth dismantling carefully, because it appears in technical discussions constantly. Temperature at zero narrows sampling but does not make generation deterministic, and the docs say so plainly - which is why every serious codebase that needs consistency uses structured outputs and validation rather than a temperature setting.

C would technically satisfy the letter of the request and quietly create a worse system: a cache makes a stale answer look like a current one.

D is the overcorrection. Refusing all consistency commitments abandons a requirement that is entirely satisfiable in the part that matters.

whyWrong.B: This is the misconception the docs are most explicit about. Setting temperature to minimum does not make generation deterministic; consistent output comes from constrained formats and validation in code, not from sampling settings.
whyWrong.C: Technically satisfies the request and operationally conceals a problem: a cache means a repeat request returns a historical answer rather than a newly generated one, and any correction to the underlying data is silently ignored.
whyWrong.D: Overcorrects into refusing a requirement that is largely satisfiable. Structured outputs and code-side validation can make the fields and the decision consistent; declining all commitments leaves the reviewer with nothing to rely on.

questions.mindset: Convert 'always identical' into a consistency contract: constrain what matters, document the tolerance on the rest.

questions.stem: A media company runs article summarisation through the Message Batches API, halving cost. The editorial director asks for a two-hour SLA on breaking-news summaries. Which response is correct?

options.text: Explain that batches are asynchronous with no completion-time guarantee - most finish within about an hour and results are available when processing ends or at 24 hours, whichever comes first. Then propose the design that meets the need: synchronous calls for breaking news, batches for everything else, with two paths and two cost profiles.
Accept the SLA. Most batches complete well inside an hour, so a two-hour commitment is realistic with margin and gives the editorial team the simplicity of one path.
Accept the SLA but submit breaking-news items in their own small batches submitted every five minutes, so the queue clears faster for high-priority content.
Decline the SLA outright and point out that batching is the only cost-effective way to summarise at this volume, leaving the editorial requirement to be renegotiated.

questions.explanation:
This is the mismatch between a **latency-tolerant optimisation and a latency requirement**, and the architect's job is to name it and then solve it rather than accept or refuse.

Batch processing is asynchronous by design: most batches complete in under an hour, results are available when processing ends or at 24 hours, and batches expire if processing does not complete. There is no completion-time guarantee you can put in an SLA. So the honest answer is that this mechanism cannot meet this requirement.

The constructive half is the point. Splitting the workload is the ordinary architectural answer: synchronous calls for breaking news at a higher unit cost, batches for the volume tail at roughly half price. That is not a compromise - it is the design that matches each class of work to the mechanism that suits it, and it makes the cost trade explicit rather than hidden.

Option C deserves a specific note, because it sounds like the sophisticated answer. Batch processing is high-throughput and concurrent; a small batch is not prioritised, so submitting it more often does not get it processed sooner. It adds queue churn and no latency benefit.

Option B is the failure mode this whole topic tests: signing an SLA against a mechanism that cannot promise it. The first missed deadline costs more trust than declining did.

whyWrong.B: Typical behaviour is not a guarantee. Batches are explicitly asynchronous and expire at 24 hours, so an SLA written against 'usually under an hour' is written against something the mechanism does not promise.
whyWrong.C: Batch processing is concurrent and high throughput, not priority-ordered. A small batch submitted more frequently is not prioritised - this adds churn without the promised speedup.
whyWrong.D: Declining without a design leaves the editorial requirement unmet and reads as obstruction. Two paths with different cost profiles is a normal architecture, not a concession.

questions.mindset: Never sign an SLA against an asynchronous mechanism - then design two paths so the requirement and the optimisation can both be met.

questions.stem: An insurer's executive sponsor wants the contract to say the assistant is '99% accurate, guaranteed on every response'. Offline evaluation on 2,000 real tickets shows 96.8%. Which response is most defensible?

options.text: Replace the per-response guarantee with a service-level objective: a measured accuracy on an agreed evaluation set plus sampled live traffic, reported monthly with an error breakdown, and an agreed remediation process when it is missed. A percentage of per-response guarantees is not something the system can attest to.
Agree to 99%. The remaining gap is small, likely closes with further prompt tuning, and refusing a number the sponsor wants damages the relationship more than a small miss rate does.
Agree to 99% but only on the offline evaluation set, and note in the contract that live accuracy may vary, since the evaluation set is the measurable figure.
Decline any accuracy commitment and explain that generative outputs are non-deterministic, so no percentage guarantee is technically possible.

questions.explanation:
The sponsor's framing contains a category error that the architect has to unpick rather than argue about: **'99% of responses' is not a quantity the system can observe or attest to.** Nobody can audit a per-response guarantee on a generative system, which means the commitment would be unverifiable even if it were met.

The construction in A is the right shape for four reasons. It names a **measurement method** - an agreed evaluation set plus sampled live traffic - so both parties know what is being measured. It makes the number **periodic and reported**, so drift becomes visible instead of discovered. It includes an **error breakdown**, so a 3% miss concentrated in medical escalation is visibly different from 3% spread across tone complaints. And it includes a **remediation process**, which is what the sponsor actually needs: what happens when it is missed.

Note the honest detail: 96.8% measured on 2,000 real tickets is a good result, and saying so plainly is part of making this credible rather than merely cautious.

D is the tempting overcorrection. Non-determinism means outputs vary run to run - it does not prevent you measuring accuracy across a large sample, which is exactly what the evaluation set is for. Refusing all commitment would leave the sponsor with no basis for the purchase.

whyWrong.B: This concedes a number the system cannot attest to, in order to avoid a conversation. The cost is a contractual commitment that is unverifiable and that will be measured - by whoever notices the first bad case - against a figure nobody agreed how to compute.
whyWrong.C: Better than B, and still wrong: it keeps the 99% figure rather than resolving whether it is measurable. The honest move is to replace the per-response framing with a measurement method, not to attach a caveat to an unattainable commitment.
whyWrong.D: Overcorrects. Non-determinism concerns variation between runs of the same input; it does not prevent measuring accuracy across thousands of labelled examples, which is precisely how the 96.8% figure was produced.

questions.mindset: Replace unmeasurable per-response promises with an SLO: method, cadence, breakdown, remediation.

questions.stem: Eight months after launch, nobody on the team can explain why the retrieval design uses a fixed chunk size of 800 tokens with 100-token overlap. A new architect inherits the system. Which documentation artefact addresses this most directly?

options.text: An architecture decision record for the chunking choice: the context, the options considered, the decision, and its consequences - including what a different chunk size would trade off. The decision's rationale is the thing that decays, not the parameter value.
A configuration reference listing every tunable parameter and its current value, so the next architect can see and change them.
Detailed inline code comments at the chunking implementation explaining how the algorithm works.
A copy of the original design review's slide deck, preserved in the team's shared drive.

questions.explanation:
The failure described is **loss of rationale**, and the artefact designed to preserve rationale is the decision record. It answers the question nobody can now answer - why 800 and 100 - by recording the context, the alternatives considered, the decision and, most valuably, its consequences. The consequence section is what makes it forward-looking: it tells the next architect what would have to be true for a different value to be right.

Worth noting what an ADR is not. It is not a record of *what* the system does - that is the configuration reference and the code, and it is exactly as accurate today as it was yesterday. Rationale is the part that decays: it lived in people's heads and in a meeting, and it is gone.

The rejected options each capture something real and miss the target. A configuration reference tells the new architect what is set without telling them whether it is right, which is why reading one does not answer the question. Code comments explain the mechanism rather than the choice. And a slide deck records what was presented to a room, not what was decided and why - which is a different artefact with a shorter shelf life than people assume.

whyWrong.B: Accurate but silent. A parameter listing tells you what is set and nothing about whether it is appropriate, so it cannot answer 'why 800' - and the value is already visible in the repository.
whyWrong.C: Comments explain mechanics. The interesting content here is why this mechanic and not another, which is a decision and belongs in a decision record.
whyWrong.D: A deck captures a presentation, not a decision with consequences. It is also the artefact most likely to be superseded by the next set of slides without anyone noticing the reasoning was lost.

questions.mindset: Parameters live in config; rationale lives in a decision record - only one of those decays silently.

questions.stem: A platform team maintains three agents that share a codebase. Each keeps its own CLAUDE.md, and an architect proposes consolidating conventions into one root CLAUDE.md. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: Consolidate what genuinely applies everywhere - build and test commands, shared error-handling conventions, the folder layout - into the root CLAUDE.md, and keep agent-specific guidance with the agent that needs it. Everything loaded in every session is a cost in every session, and agent-specific rules in a shared file are rules the wrong agents follow.
Consolidate everything into the root CLAUDE.md. A single source of truth prevents the three files from drifting, which is the main risk with separate files.
Keep the three files separate and add a note to each pointing at the other two, so nothing is lost while each agent keeps what it needs.
Consolidate the shared conventions into a single document and import it into each agent's CLAUDE.md with an `@` reference, so each file stays short while the content stays in one place.

questions.explanation:
The design principle is **relevance per context**, and it cuts both ways. CLAUDE.md content is loaded into context for the sessions in scope, so a shared file is a per-session cost for every rule it contains - including the rules that are irrelevant to the agent reading it. Meanwhile the failure the question implies, drift between files, is not solved by merging: it is solved by having exactly one copy of each convention.

A achieves both. Shared, always-applicable conventions - build commands, test invocation, the error-handling pattern, the folder layout - get one home in the root file and are loaded by every agent that works in this repository. Agent-specific guidance stays with the agent, where it is loaded only when that agent runs.

Option B optimises for the wrong failure. It eliminates drift by eliminating distinction, at the cost of every agent loading every other agent's rules. Option C preserves the problem the architect was trying to solve. Option D is the subtle one: an `@` import pulls the referenced content **into** context, so it improves navigability for humans while loading exactly as much as consolidating would. That makes D a reasonable readability choice and a poor answer to a context-cost question.

whyWrong.B: Merging removes drift by removing distinction. Each agent then loads rules written for other agents, and the shared file becomes the place where agent-specific detail accumulates because there is nowhere else obvious to put it.
whyWrong.C: Cross-references preserve the duplication that causes drift - the three files can still say different things about the same convention, and now there are pointers to reconcile as well.
whyWrong.D: `@` imports load the referenced content into context. The file gets shorter for a human reader while the model sees exactly as much as a consolidated file, so this solves navigation rather than context cost.

questions.mindset: One home per convention, loaded where it is relevant - shared in the root file, specific beside its agent.

questions.stem: A consultancy is handing a production claims-triage agent to the client's operations team, who were not involved in building it. Which TWO artefacts matter most for that handoff? Choose TWO.

options.text: A runbook: the signals to monitor and their alert thresholds, the common failure modes with their symptoms, how to tell a rate limit from a bad prompt, and how to roll back a change that degraded quality.
The evaluation suite with its baseline results and instructions for running it, because it is the only artefact that lets the receiving team verify a change is safe before shipping it.
A full export of the development chat transcripts, so the receiving team can trace how each part of the system was arrived at.
A statement that the prompts are final and must not be edited by the receiving team, since the system has been validated as delivered.
A slide deck summarising the target architecture for the receiving team's executive sponsor.

questions.explanation:
A handoff has one job: **transfer the ability to operate and change the system safely.** Two artefacts do that.

A is operational competence. The receiving team inherits a system whose failure modes they have never seen. Knowing that elevated input latency with normal quality means the provider is rate-limiting, and that a sudden drop in extraction accuracy after a prompt edit means the edit - those are the distinctions that separate a five-minute fix from an afternoon of flailing. Alert thresholds matter for the same reason: they encode what 'normal' looked like when someone who knew the system was watching.

B is the change-safety mechanism, and it is the one most handovers omit. Once the prompts and configuration are editable - and they must be, because the business will need changes - the receiving team needs a way to know a change is safe. The evaluation suite is that mechanism, and the baseline results are what make a comparison possible. Without it, the first change is an unmonitored production experiment.

The rejected options each substitute a record of the past for a capability. Transcripts and decks document what happened. D is actively harmful: freezing prompts is not a validation strategy, it is a guarantee that the first necessary change happens in production without anyone able to check it.

whyWrong.C: Transcripts record how decisions were discussed, including approaches that were abandoned. They are unbounded in volume and offer the receiving team no way to verify a change.
whyWrong.D: This removes the receiving team's ability to make necessary changes and guarantees the first real change ships without an eval gate. Validation is a process the team owns, not a state the artefact is frozen in.
whyWrong.E: An executive deck communicates value; it does not transfer operational or change capability. Useful as an addition for the sponsor, not as a handover artefact.

questions.mindset: A handoff transfers the ability to operate and change safely - runbook plus eval suite, not a record of the past.

questions.stem: A claims-summarisation service is being handed to a new team. The build team will remain available for questions for two weeks. Which handover practice most reduces the risk of a silent decline in quality after handoff?

options.text: Have the receiving team own a real change - run the evaluation suite, propose a modification, and ship it themselves - while the build team is still reachable. This surfaces missing documentation and missing understanding while the people who wrote the system can still answer.
Run a two-hour walkthrough with the receiving team, covering the architecture, the prompts and the main design decisions, and record it for reference.
Keep the build team on call for the first quarter as primary support, so the receiving team can escalate anything they cannot resolve.
Have each lead on the receiving team sign a document confirming they have read the architecture documentation and understood the system.

questions.explanation:
This is the difference between a **handover** and a **transfer**, and it is the most consequential item on this topic.

Documentation conveys what was intended. It cannot convey what was assumed, which failure modes seemed unlikely, or why a particular threshold was chosen because nothing failed. A walkthrough (B) is better than documentation because it is interactive, and it is still second-best because people nod. Sign-off (D) records that someone read something. Continued support (C) defers the problem past the point where anyone still remembers the reasoning.

A is different in kind because it **generates evidence**. When the receiving team tries to make a real change, they discover what the documentation does not cover - usually that a deployment step is implicit, or that a threshold is load-bearing for a reason nobody wrote down. Finding that out with the original author in the room is exactly the moment it is cheap to fix. Finding it in month three, with nobody to ask, is how quality degrades quietly.

This is worth stating as a principle: the residual risk in a handoff is not what was written down, it is what was never written down - and the only way to find that out is to have someone try to use the system.

whyWrong.B: A walkthrough transfers what the build team thinks to say. What it cannot transfer is what they assumed without noticing - the implicit deployment steps and load-bearing thresholds that a new operator discovers only by trying to change something.
whyWrong.C: Keeping the authors available is helpful but does not build the receiving team's capability, and it leaves the system dependent on people who are meant to leave. The goal is independence, not a long tail of escalation.
whyWrong.D: Sign-off evidences reading, not understanding, and reading a document is not evidence that the recipient could safely change the system. It is a process artefact rather than a test.

questions.mindset: The risk in a handoff is what was never written down - surface it by having the new team ship a real change.

questions.stem: A routing assistant has run for six months. Uptime is 99.95%, API error rates flat, complaints low. Last month a new home-services product line launched and misroutes to its queue have been rising steadily. Which TWO monitoring changes address this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Scheduled grading of a sample of production traffic against the eval rubric, which converts an invisible semantic failure into a number with a trend you can alert on.
Tracking of business signals such as time-to-resolution and re-routing rate per queue, which typically move earlier and are cheaper to interpret than an accuracy figure computed days later.
Tighter alerting on p95 latency broken down by queue, so the team is notified as soon as the new product line begins affecting response times.
A weekly complaint-volume alert per queue, firing when complaints rise more than 20% against the trailing average.
A daily alert on average input and output tokens per request by queue, so unusual model behaviour surfaces quickly.

questions.explanation:
The symptom - a semantic failure that is technically healthy - is the whole diagnosis. Nothing is down, nothing is slow, nobody is complaining loudly enough to trigger anything. Yet routing accuracy is degrading for one product line, and **this class of failure is invisible to infrastructure monitoring by construction**.

**A** is therefore the control that has to exist: grade a sample of production traffic on a schedule against the same rubric used in evaluation. That converts an invisible failure into a trend, and it is the only way to know whether misroutes are rising for the new product line specifically.

**B** matters for a practical reason worth stating. Business signals move earlier than a computed accuracy figure and cost less to interpret - a rising re-route rate is visible in days, a sampled accuracy score on a slower cycle. Together they give you detection inside a sample cycle rather than at the next quarterly review, which is the difference between fixing a prompt and explaining a quarter of misrouted tickets.

The rejected options each measure something real that is not moving in this scenario. Latency, complaint volume and token counts would all be flat - which is exactly why they are the wrong instruments for this failure mode.

whyWrong.C: Technical health is not in question here - uptime and error rates are explicitly fine. A latency alert fires on a symptom that does not occur while the actual problem proceeds unmonitored.
whyWrong.D: Complaint volume is a lagging signal measured in weeks and it undercounts users who simply retry. By the time it moves, the product line has been misrouting long enough to shape customer expectations.
whyWrong.E: Token counts change when inputs or outputs change, not when a routing decision becomes wrong. The misroutes here are well-formed outputs of the wrong kind - technically normal, semantically wrong.

questions.mindset: A technically healthy system can still fail semantically - measure quality on a schedule, not only infrastructure.

questions.stem: A claims-assistant prompt has passed the full evaluation suite and beats the current version. The team wants the lowest-risk release. Which TWO changes reduce risk most? Choose TWO.

options.text: Send a slice of live traffic to the new prompt first and compare its monitoring signals - accuracy on sampled traffic, escalation rate, user complaints - against the incumbent before completing the rollout.
Keep the previous prompt in version control alongside the new one so the release can be reverted quickly and the two can be diffed.
Bundle the pending model upgrade into the same release, so the team ships one change instead of two and stakeholders see a single event.
Edit the prompt directly in the production console so the improvement reaches users immediately, and document the change afterwards.
Skip further production comparison, since a prompt that passes the full evaluation suite cannot plausibly behave differently in production.

questions.explanation:
Two different kinds of risk reduction, and the release is the moment to apply both.

**A** addresses the gap an evaluation suite structurally cannot cover: it measures on the distribution you curated, and production traffic contains inputs the eval set does not have. A traffic split is how you discover a prompt that scores beautifully on the test set and behaves differently on the long tail. It also gives a rollback trigger - if the sampled accuracy or the escalation rate moves against the incumbent, you stop.

**B** is the prerequisite that makes any rollback possible. Keeping the previous prompt in version control rather than in someone's memory means reverting is a deployment, not an archaeology project. It also gives you a diff when something goes wrong later, which is how you find out what actually shipped.

The rejected options cluster around a common error - treating release as a single event to be managed rather than a sequence with reversible steps. C bundles an unrelated change so that if quality drops you cannot tell which one caused it. D bypasses version control entirely, which is what B exists to prevent. E treats the eval suite as total coverage when it is by definition a sample of what exists.

whyWrong.C: Bundling an unrelated model upgrade destroys attribution. If quality or latency moves after the release, two variables changed at once and neither can be isolated without a second deployment.
whyWrong.D: Editing in the production console leaves no version record, so the previous prompt is recoverable only from someone's memory, and a bad edit has no revert path.
whyWrong.E: An evaluation suite is a curated sample by construction. Production traffic contains inputs it does not, which is exactly the population a passing score says nothing about.

questions.mindset: Release behind a traffic split with a versioned rollback path - one change at a time, so a regression is attributable.

questions.stem: A pilot of an invoice-coding assistant in one region scored 85% correct general-ledger codes against a 92% target agreed in discovery. The CFO is impressed with the time savings and wants a full rollout. The architect's report to the steering committee contains four sections. Which structure is most defensible?

options.text: The gap against the agreed target with the error breakdown by category and region; the cause, evidenced rather than speculated; costed options to close the gap with their timelines; and a recommendation on whether to expand, hold, or expand in a specific region - with the expansion gate stated as the metric it will be measured on.
Headline the time savings achieved in the pilot, then present the accuracy shortfall against target as an item still in progress, since both facts are true and the savings are the business case.
Report the gap honestly without the time savings, and recommend the team hold expansion until the target is met, since accuracy is the metric that was agreed.
Revise the target to 85% and present a rollout plan against it, since the pilot result is the most realistic available estimate of field performance.

questions.explanation:
This question is about **accountability under a target that was missed**, and the structure that survives scrutiny is the one that presents the whole picture and still makes a decision.

A's four parts each do a job. The gap with a **breakdown by category and region** shows whether this is uniform under-performance or concentrated - 85% overall with 79% on the largest region is a different problem from 85% everywhere, and only the breakdown distinguishes them. **Cause evidenced rather than speculated** is what separates a diagnosis from an excuse, and it is what lets the committee evaluate the options. **Costed options with timelines** convert 'we missed' into 'here is what closing it costs and when', which is the only form in which a committee can decide. And the recommendation names a **specific expansion gate as a metric**, so expansion becomes conditional and measurable rather than a matter of momentum.

The rejected options each handle the missed target by hiding or relocating it. B front-loads the favourable number and files the shortfall as work in progress - true, and structurally a way of not reporting it. C is honest but incomplete: reporting a gap with no options gives the committee nothing to decide, and the time savings are real and relevant to whether expansion is worth it at all. D quietly changes the target to match the result, which is the one move a steering committee cannot allow without an explicit discussion.

whyWrong.B: Presenting both facts is not the problem; the ordering is. Leading with the favourable number and filing a missed agreed target as in-progress work is a way of reporting around it, and the committee cannot see the trade-off it is being asked to make.
whyWrong.C: Honest but not actionable. A report that states a gap and stops leaves the committee with nothing to decide, and it omits the time savings that bear directly on whether expansion is worthwhile at 85%.
whyWrong.D: Changing the target to match the measured result removes the committee's decision. If the target can move whenever it is missed, it was not a target - and any revision has to be an explicit, argued committee decision.

questions.mindset: Report the miss in full: gap plus breakdown, evidenced cause, costed options, and a named expansion gate.

questions.stem: You are designing an agent for a legal aid charity. Two designs are on the table: a single model call with a well-written prompt, and a multi-step design with a retrieval step and a verification step. The board wants the multi-step design because it is 'more advanced'. Which TWO statements are correct? Choose TWO.

options.text: Architecture should follow the requirement. Recommend the simpler design if the pilot meets the agreed accuracy target, and state what would justify the complex one - a measured accuracy gap the simple design cannot close.
Each additional step brings its own failure mode, latency, cost and regression surface. That is an argument for tying complexity to a measured need, not an argument against it.
Build the multi-step design as requested. The board owns the budget and has stated a preference, and a board that is told its preference was declined will fund the next attempt more readily.
Deploy both behind a traffic split for a quarter and report which performs better, so the decision rests on data rather than architectural preference.
Recommend the multi-step design, since in legal aid the cost of a wrong answer borne by a tenant in arrears is high enough to justify added complexity for its own sake.

questions.explanation:
The most common failure in architecture proposals is **complexity arriving without a requirement behind it**.

**A** is the principle: architecture follows the requirement, so the simpler design stands if the pilot meets the agreed target - and the reversal condition is stated explicitly. That converts the conversation from 'do you like this architecture' into 'what would have to be true', which is the only framing a board can actually evaluate.

**B** is the part that gets skipped, and it is what makes A more than a preference. Every added step in an agentic design brings its own failure mode, latency, cost and regression surface. That does not argue against complexity; it argues that complexity must earn its place against a measured need. In a legal-aid context the stakes are exactly why the accuracy bar should be set to close the gap rather than accepted as a reason to take on unmeasured structure.

The rejected options each substitute deference or delay for analysis. C is deference, and its hidden cost is real: the next honest recommendation becomes harder to fund. D looks rigorous and usually is not - a quarter of split traffic is expensive, produces two half-proven systems, and still leaves a board that asked for complexity unconvinced even when the simple design suffices. E reaches for a genuine concern and then substitutes feeling for measurement.

whyWrong.C: Deference to a stated preference without a requirement behind it. It spends the charity's budget on steps whose value nobody demonstrated, and it makes the next honest recommendation harder to fund.
whyWrong.D: Expensive, and it does not settle the question. A quarter of split traffic gives two half-proven systems, and a result showing the simple design suffices still leaves a board that asked for complexity unconvinced.
whyWrong.E: The stakes are real and are exactly why the accuracy bar should be set to close the gap. Accepting unmeasured complexity because the domain is serious removes the mechanism that would tell you whether the complexity helped.

questions.mindset: Complexity must earn its place against a measured need - and you should name what would justify it.

questions.stem: A support assistant has run four months. Production sampling has flagged 140 failed responses this month, and the team has capacity for one focused improvement. A senior engineer proposes fixing the three failures the executive forwarded. Which response is best?

options.text: Cluster the failures by root cause, rank the clusters by frequency and business impact, and fix the largest. Three forwarded cases are three symptoms, and fixing a symptom rarely removes its cluster - while the top cluster may account for most of the 140.
Fix the executive's cases first. Visibility with leadership is a finite resource, and a fix they can see creates the confidence that funds the next quarter's work.
Rewrite the system prompt from scratch to address all 140 failures at once, since they likely share a root cause in the prompt.
Upgrade to a more capable model, since a stronger model is likely to resolve a large share of the failures without any analysis.

questions.explanation:
This is the **queue** problem, and the discipline is the same as any service queue: work the highest-impact item, not the loudest one.

Clustering by root cause is what converts 140 incidents into a handful of addressable problems. Three forwarded cases are three *symptoms* - and the reason they reached an executive is often that they were the most confusing, not the most common. Fixing a symptom does not remove its cluster; the same underlying cause keeps producing it, at whatever rate it produces it.

Ranking by frequency times business impact then does the real work. A cluster responsible for 90 of 140 failures, or for low customer effort, is worth more than three individually memorable cases. And clustering produces something the forwarded cases never will: a statement about *why* the system fails, which is what makes the next iteration faster.

The rejected options each substitute visibility, drastic action or capability for analysis. B optimises for the story rather than the customer. C is the most tempting because it feels decisive - and a full rewrite discards whatever was working, changes behaviour everywhere, and cannot be attributed if it regresses. D spends the iteration budget on a change that might fix much, all, or none of it.

whyWrong.B: Optimises for visibility rather than customers. Three forwarded cases are symptoms chosen partly for being confusing, and fixing them leaves their root causes producing the next three.
whyWrong.C: Feels decisive and destroys attribution. A full rewrite discards working behaviour, changes the system everywhere, and if quality moves afterwards nobody can tell which change caused it - and it may not even be the cause of the 140.
whyWrong.D: Spends the iteration budget on an unmeasured change. A model upgrade might resolve much, all or none of the failures, and it changes behaviour across every cluster at once without telling you which cause mattered.

questions.mindset: Cluster failures by root cause and work the biggest - loud cases are symptoms, not priorities.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, the HR director asks the benefits assistant to 'also submit leave requests on employees' behalf'. The assistant currently only answers questions. Which response is most defensible?

options.text: Treat it as a new capability rather than a feature request: run discovery on approvals, permissions, data handling and what happens when a request is wrong, then add the capability behind the controls that work implies. Scope creep into action-taking is where assistant deployments get into real incidents.
Add the submission tool next sprint as proposed. The underlying assistant already understands leave policy correctly, so the capability is a natural extension of what it does.
Decline the request. The original discovery scoped the assistant to answering questions only, and re-opening scope is a governance failure.
Design a separate autonomous multi-agent system for HR transactions with its own planner, executor and verifier, since transaction handling is architecturally different from question answering.

questions.explanation:
The gap between **answering about** a process and **acting in** it is where the risk lives, and it is worth naming precisely. An assistant that explains the leave policy can be wrong in a way a user notices and corrects. An assistant that submits a leave request can be wrong in a way that lands in someone's payslip, and the user may not see it for a month.

So this is a new capability with new questions: who approves, what the agent may and may not do without approval, what it can see, what happens when a request is wrong or duplicated, and what the reversal path is. Those are discovery questions, not implementation details, and answering them after building is how the wrong thing gets shipped.

The rejected options each skip that step. B assumes understanding a policy implies authority to act on it - the confidence is warranted, the conclusion is not. C treats scope as closed, when a business asking for a natural extension is a legitimate input; refusing on governance grounds without a conversation is its own failure.

D is the overcorrection, and it is worth naming the failure mode it represents: reaching for a large multi-agent architecture when the actual work is discovering the approval model. If a tool call with an approval gate and an audit trail does the job, a planner-executor-verifier system adds coordination failure modes and cost without addressing anything discovery would have told you.

whyWrong.B: Understanding a policy and being authorised to act on it are different capabilities. Nothing in the current design addresses approvals, duplicate submissions, or what happens when a submitted request is wrong.
whyWrong.C: Declining without a conversation treats a legitimate business request as a governance violation. The right response is to scope it properly, and if the answer is still no, that is a decision made with reasons rather than by default.
whyWrong.D: A planner-executor-verifier architecture answers a question nobody asked. The open problems here are approvals and reversibility, which discovery resolves and additional agents do not.

questions.mindset: Acting on a process is a new capability with new risk - re-open discovery before you add a tool.

questions.stem: A document-extraction system has run in production for a year on a pinned Claude model. Anthropic has emailed that the model is deprecated and will be retired in two months, with a recommended replacement. Which TWO actions are correct? Choose TWO.

options.text: Run the existing evaluation suite against the recommended replacement and compare quality, latency and cost against the incumbent. You already have the instrument, and it makes the comparison interpretable.
Read the migration notes for breaking changes and roll out gradually behind a traffic split with a rollback path, so a regression is a small reversible event rather than an outage.
Change the model identifier in configuration on the retirement date, since Anthropic documents the replacement as the migration path.
Keep the current model running until requests begin failing after retirement, then migrate - avoiding engineering time on a change the provider has already specified.
Rewrite the prompts from scratch for the new model, since prompts are tuned to a specific model and unlikely to carry over.

questions.explanation:
A deprecation notice with a date is a **scheduled project**, and treating it as one is worth more than any particular technique here.

**A** is the evaluation step: you already have the instrument, and running it against the candidate is what makes the comparison interpretable. Note the three dimensions - a recommended replacement is not automatically better on the ones your SLA is written against, particularly latency.

**B** covers the two things that catch teams out. Reading the migration notes surfaces breaking changes while there is still time to fix them; rolling out gradually with a rollback path makes any regression small and reversible instead of an outage.

The rejected options each buy speed with a larger risk. C substitutes a vendor recommendation for your own measurement - the recommended model is a sound default, not a validated one for your workload. D converts a planned two-month migration into an emergency during an incident, with degraded service for every user in the interval. And E's premise is worth examining directly: prompts do not generally need rewriting between model generations, they need *checking*. A rewrite by assumption discards working prompt engineering and changes every variable at once, so if the migration does expose a problem you will not be able to tell which change caused it.

whyWrong.C: A vendor recommendation is a sound default and not a validation. It tells you nothing about accuracy or latency on your workload, and adopting it unmeasured means any regression is found in production.
whyWrong.D: Turns a planned migration into an outage. Two months of runway exists precisely so the work can be done with evaluation and a staged rollout rather than during an incident with users affected.
whyWrong.E: Prompts generally carry across model generations and need checking rather than rewriting. A rewrite discards working prompt engineering and changes every variable at once, so any regression becomes untraceable.

questions.mindset: A deprecation date is a scheduled project - evaluate the candidate on your own suite, then roll out with a rollback path.

questions.stem: Five product teams are each building their own Claude-based summarisation feature from the architect's written implementation guide. Six months later the review finds five retry strategies, four logging formats, three prompt structures and one team with no evaluation suite. Which TWO changes most improve consistency? Choose TWO.

options.text: A maintained reference implementation - a template repository with retries using capped backoff honouring retry-after, structured logging carrying request id and usage, and a working eval harness - so teams copy a pattern rather than interpret one.
A definition of done requiring the agreed eval suite to pass in CI before release, which converts 'the guide said to have evals' into a check that can fail a build.
A longer written guide describing retries, logging and evaluation in more detail, with additional worked examples for each pattern.
A central architecture team that writes every team's prompts and code on their behalf, so the implementation is consistent by construction.
A rule that every team must use the most capable model, so at least the model choice is consistent across all five features.

questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is a **transfer** problem, not an awareness problem. Five teams read the same guide and produced five different implementations, which means the guide conveyed principles without making decisions. The question is what artefact closes that gap.

**A** makes the right pattern executable. A team can copy working retry handling that honours `retry-after` with capped backoff, logging carrying request id, `stop_reason` and usage, and an eval harness that runs - which removes the interpretive step where each team decided for itself what 'use exponential backoff' meant.

**B** is what makes it stick. An eval suite passing in CI before release is a gate rather than a recommendation, and it means divergence becomes visible at the point where it would otherwise ship. The two halves reinforce: the template makes the right thing easy, the gate makes skipping it expensive.

The rejected options each treat the symptom. More prose deepens the problem - the teams were not unaware of the guidance, each interpreted it differently, and more description gives more room for interpretation. Central authorship removes independent shipping and creates a bottleneck. And a rule about model tier standardises the parameter most likely to differ by each team's own evidence, which inverts the intent.

whyWrong.C: More prose deepens the problem. The teams were not unaware of the guidance; each interpreted it differently, and additional description gives more more room for interpretation rather than less.
whyWrong.D: Removes every team's ability to ship independently and creates a central bottleneck. Consistency by central authorship also means queueing behind one team, and builds no capability in the teams that must operate these systems.
whyWrong.E: Standardising on the most capable tier ignores that each team has its own workload, volume and quality bar. Consistency on the parameter most likely to differ by evidence inverts the intent - and it is the most expensive way to be consistent.

questions.mindset: Guides convey principles, not decisions - ship a reference implementation plus a CI gate teams can fail.

questions.stem: A hospital is rolling out a discharge-summary drafting assistant to 40 nurses, most of whom are not technical. The architecture and runbooks are complete and thorough. Early pilot users either over-trust the drafts or ignore them entirely, and the clinical lead asks what is missing. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Nurses need a different artefact: a short guide to what the tool does and does not do, what to check in each draft, and what to escalate when a summary looks wrong. Operational guidance for a non-technical audience is not the architecture document - it answers a different question.
The team should increase adoption by training nurses to rely on the drafts more confidently, since the assistant's measured accuracy makes reliance the safe default.
The team should restrict the tool to the nurses who have completed advanced training, so that only users who understand its limitations have access.
Nothing further is needed. The architecture and runbooks are complete, so the remaining variance in how users respond is a training matter for the clinical lead to handle locally.

questions.explanation:
The architecture document and the thing a nurse needs at 7am are **answers to different questions**. One describes how the system is built and operated; the other tells a user what it does, what it does not do, what to check in every draft, and what to escalate. Nurses do not need the retrieval architecture - they need to know that a medication list is the field most worth checking, and that a confident-sounding summary of a complicated discharge is exactly when to call the ward pharmacist.

This is a general pattern in documentation, and it is worth naming because the artefact that exists is not a substitute. A team that has written a thorough architecture document can conclude it is done; what it has actually done is answer a question nobody on the ward asked.

The rejected options each substitute a different remedy for a documentation gap. B pushes reliance without addressing what the user should verify - and training people to rely on output they do not know how to check is how a bad summary reaches a patient. C gates access on technical sophistication rather than supplying the guidance that makes the tool usable. D treats a documentation-design problem as local training and leaves new users with nothing.

whyWrong.B: Training for confidence without telling users what to check is the failure mode in waiting. A nurse who does not know which fields are risky has no basis for scrutiny, and a wrong summary then travels to a patient unchallenged.
whyWrong.C: Gates access on technical sophistication rather than supplying the guidance that makes the tool usable. The tool's value is to reduce workload, so excluding most of the ward removes most of the benefit and solves a documentation problem with an access restriction.
whyWrong.D: Treats a documentation-design problem as local training. The runbooks answer an operator's question, and a nurse at the bedside has a different one; new users arriving after the pilot get nothing.

questions.mindset: Match the artefact to the audience's question - an architecture document does not tell a nurse what to check.
